name: Coins 1, 3, 4
why: 6: greedy gives 4 + 1 + 1, but 3 + 3 is two coins. Every smaller amount is fine.

name: Coins 1, 10, 25
why: 30: greedy gives 25 + five 1s (6 coins), but 10 + 10 + 10 is 3. The first failure is above the largest coin, so checking only up to 25 misses it.

name: Only the 1
why: None: with one coin there is only one way to pay.

name: Two coins
why: None: with coins 1 and c, the largest coin first is always best.

name: Coins 1, 5, 12
why: 15: greedy gives 12 + 1 + 1 + 1, but 5 + 5 + 5 is three coins.

name: Powers of two
why: None: when each coin is double the one before, the largest coin first is always best, so no amount fails.

name: Not in order
why: 6: sort the coins first; the list may come in any order.

name: A failure far away
why: 20000: greedy takes 10001 and then 9,999 coins of 1; two 10000s are enough. Below 20000 greedy is always best. Fill a table of the fewest coins for each amount; searching each amount separately is far too slow.

name: A large canonical system
why: None. Every amount below 150,000 (the two largest coins) must be checked, so the table has 150,000 entries. Checking further, for example up to the largest coin squared, is far too slow.
